metadata.eval_design_note: Iteration-1 uses 12 direct content-quality evals covering specification correctness, pushback on bad models, brevity calibration, and triggering. Each expectation is a specific, objectively checkable assertion. Both configurations score 100% — a full ceiling effect. The base model answers direct MLM questions correctly; the skill's behavioral value (changing defaults when a user presents a wrong analysis as apparently acceptable) is not captured by these prompts. Iteration-2 will use trap-based prompts where the user presents a flawed analysis and asks for validation.

expectations.text: Identifies subjects and items as crossed random effects, not nested
expectations.evidence: Explicitly states 'they are crossed, not nested: every participant read every sentence' and uses two separate random-effect terms (1 + ambiguity | participant) + (1 | item), which is the crossed specification.

expectations.text: Includes a by-subject random slope for the ambiguity manipulation
expectations.evidence: Formula includes (1 + ambiguity | participant) and the text explicitly explains why this slope is necessary.

expectations.text: Includes a by-item random slope for the ambiguity manipulation IF items appear in both conditions (within-items design), OR correctly explains that a by-item slope is not estimable because ambiguity is a between-items property in this design
expectations.evidence: The response correctly explains that a by-item slope is not estimable: 'No by-item random slope for ambiguity: ambiguity does not vary within items (each sentence is fixed as ambiguous or unambiguous), so a by-item random slope is not estimable.' This is the correct application of the maximal-model principle — include slopes only where the predictor varies within the grouping factor. Expectation updated to accept the correct 'between-items' explanation as passing.

expectations.text: Does NOT recommend a random-intercepts-only model like (1 | subject)
expectations.evidence: Explicitly states 'Do not use (1 | participant) alone — that random-intercepts-only model omits the by-participant slope, inflates Type I error, and is almost never defensible for within-subjects manipulations.'

expectations.text: References the rationale for random slopes for within-cluster manipulations (Barr et al. 2013 / inflated Type I error / Keep It Maximal)
expectations.evidence: Cites 'Barr, Levy, Scheepers & Tily, 2013 — Keep It Maximal' and states 'false-positive rates of 20–50% at nominal α = .05 when random slopes are omitted.'

expectations.text: Identifies subjects and items as crossed random effects, not nested
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly states 'subjects and items are crossed because every subject reads multiple items, and every item is read by multiple subjects' and uses (1 + ambiguity | subject) + (1 | item) syntax, explicitly warning 'Do not nest items within subjects.'

expectations.text: Includes a by-subject random slope for the ambiguity manipulation
expectations.evidence: Response includes (1 + ambiguity | subject) in the recommended model and explains the rationale: ambiguity is within-subject so slope heterogeneity across participants must be modeled.

expectations.text: Includes a by-item random slope for the ambiguity manipulation IF items appear in both conditions (within-items design), OR correctly explains that a by-item slope is not estimable because ambiguity is a between-items property in this design
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly explains: 'Each sentence is fixed as either ambiguous or unambiguous — ambiguity is a between-items property. A given item does not appear in both conditions, so there is no within-item variance in ambiguity to estimate a slope over... Including (1 + ambiguity | item) would be asking the model to estimate how the effect of ambiguity varies across items that only ever experienced one level of the factor — this is not identified.' This is a correct and complete explanation.

expectations.text: Does NOT recommend a random-intercepts-only model like (1 | subject)
expectations.evidence: Response recommends (1 + ambiguity | subject), explicitly warns against (1 | subject) only: 'Omitting this slope and using only (1 | subject) would inflate Type I error for the ambiguity fixed effect.'

expectations.text: References the rationale for random slopes for within-cluster manipulations (Barr et al. 2013 / inflated Type I error / Keep It Maximal)
expectations.evidence: Response cites 'Barr et al. (2013, Journal of Memory and Language)' by name, mentions 'inflate Type I error', and quotes the 'Keep It Maximal' principle directly.

expectations.text: Identifies the three-level nested structure
expectations.evidence: Explicitly maps all 3 levels: 'Level 1 = repeated measurements (time points nested within students), Level 2 = students nested within schools, Level 3 = schools (where the intervention was assigned).'

expectations.text: Flags that 25 schools is small for level-3 inference
expectations.evidence: '25 schools is small for level-3 inference. CRSE is known to be unreliable below ~30–50 clusters; with only 25 schools the sandwich variance estimator can be anti-conservative or overly conservative.'

expectations.text: Suggests MLM as preferred but engages with the OLS+CRSE alternative honestly
expectations.evidence: 'MLM is preferred but CRSE is not wrong if you only want a population-average treatment effect and cluster at the school level. But it ignores the repeated-measures structure, gives no ICC/variance components, and has those small-sample weaknesses.' — honest engagement with both options.

expectations.text: Mentions Bayesian estimation as an option for small-cluster regimes, OR Kenward-Roger / small-sample corrections
expectations.evidence: Both covered: Kenward-Roger df via anova(fit, ddf = "Kenward-Roger") in lmerTest, and brms with weakly informative priors framed as 'the preferred route when cluster counts are in the 5–30 range.'

expectations.text: Identifies the three-level nested structure
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly labels the three levels: measurements (level 1) nested within students (level 2) nested within schools (level 3), and notes that OLS+CRSE collapses this hierarchy and cannot partition variance across levels.

expectations.text: Flags that 25 schools is small for level-3 inference
expectations.evidence: Response directly states '25 schools is a small number of level-3 units,' references the 30–50 cluster rule of thumb, cites Cameron & Miller (2015), and explains that the sandwich estimator is unreliable at n=25 clusters.

expectations.text: Suggests MLM as preferred but engages with the OLS+CRSE alternative honestly
expectations.evidence: Response calls MLM 'the preferred approach,' explains why, but also engages honestly with CRSE: acknowledges it as 'a reasonable starting point,' describes the specific failure mode (downward bias at small cluster counts), and suggests CR2-corrected CRSE as an acceptable robustness check rather than dismissing it entirely.

expectations.text: Mentions Bayesian estimation as an option for small-cluster regimes, OR Kenward-Roger / small-sample corrections
expectations.evidence: Response mentions both: Kenward-Roger degrees-of-freedom corrections (with specific software references: lme4 + pbkrtest, SAS PROC MIXED) and Bayesian estimation via brms/Stan, with explanation of why each is appropriate for small level-3 sample sizes.

expectations.text: Identifies this as a cluster-randomized / cluster-RCT design
expectations.evidence: Opening sentence: 'Your design is a cluster-randomized trial (cluster RCT): treatment is assigned at the clinic level, not the patient level.'

expectations.text: Notes that the relevant n is the number of clusters (30), not total patients
expectations.evidence: 'The binding constraint is the number of clusters (clinics), not total patients.' And: 'For the treatment effect (a between-clinic effect), power scales with the number of clinics, not total N.'

expectations.text: Recommends simulation-based power analysis (e.g., simr) or otherwise gives MLM-appropriate power guidance — NOT a t-test power calculator
expectations.evidence: Explicitly warns 'Do not use G*Power or similar OLS-based tools without a multilevel module' and recommends 'simr in R' by name.

expectations.text: Mentions ICC as an input to power
expectations.evidence: ICC appears in the design effect formula (n_eff = n_total / (1 + (m-1) × ICC)), in the numerical example, and as a named required key input with suggested ranges.

expectations.text: Asks for or specifies an assumed effect size rather than computing power on a pilot estimate uncritically
expectations.evidence: 'Do not rely on a pilot estimate uncritically — pilot estimates are typically noisy and upwardly biased. Power on the smallest effect that would be clinically meaningful.'

expectations.text: Identifies this as a cluster-randomized / cluster-RCT design
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly states 'This is a cluster-randomized controlled trial (cluster-RCT) design — treatment is assigned at the clinic level, so the clinic is your unit of randomization.'

expectations.text: Notes that the relevant n is the number of clusters (30), not total patients
expectations.evidence: Response states 'The relevant n is the number of clusters (30 clinics), not the total number of patients (600)' and explains that patients within a clinic are not independent.

expectations.text: Recommends simulation-based power analysis (e.g., simr) or otherwise gives MLM-appropriate power guidance — NOT a t-test power calculator
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly recommends simr for simulation-based power, also mentions clusterPower and analytic cluster-RCT formulas, and specifically says 'not a standard t-test calculator.'

expectations.text: Mentions ICC as an input to power
expectations.evidence: Response devotes a full point to ICC, defines it, gives the design effect formula DEFF = 1 + (m−1) × ICC, and lists it as a required input with typical value ranges.

expectations.text: Asks for or specifies an assumed effect size rather than computing power on a pilot estimate uncritically
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly warns 'don't just use a pilot estimate uncritically, as pilot ICCs and effect sizes are noisy' and frames effect size as something to assume based on clinical meaningfulness.

expectations.text: Identifies that the model is missing a by-subject random slope for condition
expectations.evidence: 'The model lmer(rt ~ condition + (1 | subject)) is missing a by-subject random slope for condition — and condition is a within-subjects manipulation, which makes this omission consequential.'

expectations.text: Explains that this inflates Type I error for the within-subjects effect
expectations.evidence: 'the correct error term for testing the condition effect is the by-subject variability... A random-intercepts-only model doesn't estimate that variability; it pools residual variance incorrectly and produces a test statistic that is anti-conservative... The result is inflated Type I error.'

expectations.text: Walks through diagnosis before simplification

expectations.text: Recommends dropping correlation parameters (||) before dropping random slopes

expectations.text: Mentions principled simplification order (correlations first, then interaction slopes, etc.)

expectations.text: Identifies the non-unique-ID problem
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly names 'ID non-uniqueness' and explains that IDs 1–30 within each classroom means different students share the same student_id value.

expectations.text: Explains that the naive syntax would conflate students with the same ID across classrooms
expectations.evidence: 'lme4 treats all rows with student_id == 1 as belonging to the same random-effect level — effectively pooling students across classrooms who share a number... conflating students from different classrooms into spurious super-students.'

expectations.text: Recommends either globally unique IDs or the explicit nesting syntax (e.g., classroom/student_id or classroom:student_id)
expectations.evidence: Both options given explicitly: (1 | classroom/student_id) which expands to (1 | classroom) + (1 | classroom:student_id), and creating a globally unique ID via paste(d$classroom, d$student_id, sep = "_").

expectations.text: Identifies the non-unique-ID problem

expectations.text: Explains that the naive syntax would conflate students with the same ID across classrooms

expectations.text: Recommends either globally unique IDs or the explicit nesting syntax (e.g., classroom/student_id or classroom:student_id)
expectations.evidence: Provides both fixes: (1) creating globally unique IDs via paste(), and (2) using (1|classroom/student_id) or (1|classroom) + (1|classroom:student_id) with explanation of how the interaction term generates unique labels.

expectations.text: Identifies that treatment-coded 'main effects' in interaction models are simple effects, not average effects
expectations.evidence: 'the condition coefficient estimates the condition difference only at the reference level of time. It is a simple effect, not a marginal (average) effect.'
